title: 3-Read Friday #117: Principles vs Practices, Managing Call-Outs, and Big Mathematical Ideas
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #117 opens with Mark Enser arguing that CPD which prescribes practices without their underlying principles breeds 'cargo cult teaching' -- perfect-looking rituals with no real understanding behind them -- because practices are only routes, while principles are the map that lets a teacher navigate new situations. Jonathan Jarrett-Kerr then argues that praising a call-out response ('well done, but don't shout out next time') backfires, because the dopamine hit of being right lands before the correction and quietly rewards the very behaviour being discouraged, and that the better fix is to get upstream of it by reordering a single question. Colin Foster closes with a curriculum-design piece arguing that school mathematics too often becomes a fragmented 'to-do list' of procedures that are rehearsed and then forgotten, proposing instead that the whole curriculum be organised around five cross-cutting 'Big Ideas,' starting with thinking multiplicatively. Barton connects all three as different diagnoses of the same failure mode: treating surface-level technique as if it were the substance of good practice.
points: Enser's cargo-cult-teaching warning: CPD that hands teachers practices without the principles behind them produces rituals that look right but carry no real understanding, leaving teachers unable to adapt when the practice doesn't fit.

Jarrett-Kerr's call-out fix reframes the problem as sequencing, not praise wording -- since the dopamine of being right lands before any correction can land, the solution is to reorder the question itself, getting upstream of the call-out.

Foster's five 'Big Ideas' curriculum structure treats many topic-specific student struggles as the same underlying weakness (e.g., multiplicative thinking) wearing different disguises across topics, rather than genuinely separate problems.

Barton's throughline: all three posts diagnose surface-level technique -- rote practices, praise scripts, topic-by-topic procedures -- being mistaken for the substance of good teaching or good curriculum design.
quotes: The gap between doing something in the classroom and understanding why you're doing it is often large and significant.
